newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland marks another sombre milestone.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland marks another sombre milestone.

text.p: Northern Ireland marked the first anniversary of the ending of an IRA truce on Sunday with peace talks at standstill, violence on the increase and the gulf of distrust between majority Protestants and minority Catholics widening.

Ken Maginnis, security spokesman for the biggest pro-British political party, the Ulster Unionists (UUP), accused the guerrillas and their political wing, Sinn Fein, of trying to turn the province into another Bosnia of sectarian hatred.

His remarks in a weekend interview highlighted new tensions between pro-British and pro-Irish politicians on the first anniversary of the IRA bomb at London's Canary Wharf which ended a 17-month truce and wrecked brief dreams of peace.

He accused the Irish Republican Army of trying to turn Northern Ireland into sectarian ghettos through attacks on British army patrols and local police, which have occurred almost every other day since the start of this year.

According to his analysis, IRA and Sinn Fein strategy is to render Northern Ireland ungovernable so that the United Nations is called in, bypassing British insistence that the IRA end violence for good to earn a place at the peace talks' table.

"It's a violence that wants to turn this community into ghettos so that they can achieve a Bosnian-type situation where there is a standoff....to attract outside influence," he told the British Broadcasting Corporation.
"Ultimately they would like to see the United Nations involved here," said Maginnis, whose UUP is the mainstream voice of a 60 percent Protestant majority that wants to stay British.

Gerry Adams, the Sinn Fein president, insisted in weekend statements that Sinn Fein wanted to take part in Belfast peace talks which have done little but mark time since last June, but sidestepped questions about a new IRA truce.

Prime Minister John Major's British government, which faces electoral defeat at polls due by May, insists that the IRA call a new, permanent truce and prove its democratic credentials before being admitted to the negotiations.

The IRA, in a statement last week, said that it wanted to be part of the peace process but would not accept any preconditions for the involvement of Sinn Fein at talks which group Unionists and the moderate Irish nationalist SDLP party of John Hume.

But participants at the talks, which are chaired by former U.S. Senator George Mitchell, say they are just marking time until the British elections are out of the way and a new government emerges to put its stamp on Northern Ireland policy.

Security sources believe the IRA's latest campaign, which switched to Northern Ireland last October with a twin car bomb attack on Britain's army headquarters at Lisburn, which killed one soldier, is aimed at creating mayhem in Northern Ireland.

They believe the IRA is trying to goad its Protestant Loyalist foes, who waged a guerrilla war to stay British, into ending their own two-year truce so that the next government inherits a province once again at war with itself.

Communal tension was vividly illustrated on Saturday night when up to 1,000 Protestants chanting anti-Catholic abuse marched on a Catholic church at Harryville in the overwhelmingly Protestant town of Ballymena.
It was the latest round in a 23-week protest aimed at forcing Catholics in the nearby village of Dunloy to drop their opposition to a march through by the Protestant Orange Order.

The Harryville demonstration effectively kicked off the yearly "marching season" by Protestants, which last year caused the worst civil unrest in decades when police banned one of its parades after Catholic protest and then allowed it, sparking a wave of Catholic agitation instead.
